2023_021_22106a_22107a_troy_board_rooms_.paragraph: A furnishing recommendation letter and bid package prepared by TMP Architecture, Inc. for the Troy School District Central Office Board Room (TMP Project No. 22106A) and Services Building Board Room (TMP Project No. 22107A), dated August 31, 2023 and issued for Board approval. Interior designer Keri Seeney recommended awarding five furnishing categories to dealers quoting off pre-existing consortium bid contracts, for a total amount of $84,505.95. Category A, KI product supplied through Interior Office Source, is the dominant share at $74,738.10. The package bundles general conditions, a dealer code of conduct, submittal procedures, item-by-item furniture specifications, and each dealer's underlying quotation.
2023_021_22106a_22107a_troy_board_rooms_.page:
Overview
TMP Architecture, Inc. of Bloomfield Hills submitted a furnishing recommendation dated August 31, 2023 to Ms. Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Education, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098. The package covers the Troy Central Office Board Room (TMP Project No. 22106A, 4400 Livernois Road) and the Troy Services Building Board Room (TMP Project No. 22107A, 4420 Livernois Road). Quotes were obtained based on pre-existing bid contracts (consortiums). The letter is signed by Keri Seeney, NCIDQ, Associate | Interior Designer, with a copy to Laura Casai of TMP Architecture.

Category B is item B1, VS America model 01471 Team Table, 65 x 44-7/8 inches, 40 inches high, anthracite finishes, Services Building Board Room. Contract Terms
The Owner may hold quotes ninety days. Each quote must carry a notarized familial relationship disclosure under Public Act 232 of 2004, a Non-Collusion Affidavit, and a Certification of Compliance with the Iran Economic Sanctions Act (Michigan Public Act No. 517 of 2012, with a civil penalty of not more than $250,000.00 or two times the contract amount, whichever is greater, and three-year bid ineligibility for a false certification). Dealers must carry Comprehensive General Liability and Automobile Liability insurance of $1,000,000 per person and $1,000,000 per occurrence, and $1,000,000 property damage per occurrence, with thirty days written notice of cancellation and Troy School District named as insured. Delivery is between 8:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. in Fall 2023, with installation complete by Fall 2023 and a pre-installation notice issued three to four weeks ahead. Payment reaches 80 percent of the bid category after installation and the Architect's initial punch list, with the balance on final approval; invoices go to Mr. Rick West, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services. The project is not subject to prevailing wage rate requirements for Oakland County, and warranties run one year from project completion and Owner acceptance. Submittal review allows 15 working days for an initial review and 15 working days for a resubmittal.

2023_023_portrait_of_a_graduate_data_gat.paragraph: A Board presentation summarizing the data-gathering phase of the Troy School District Portrait of a Graduate exercise, drawing on parent surveys, a K-12 principals discussion, and classroom conversations with students. The research produced twelve traits expected of a Troy graduate, ranging from Visionary and Connected to Organized and Confident Communicator, and reported near-perfect overlap in the priorities named by students, parents and principals. Parent input alone comprised 308 completed surveys generating more than 24,000 words of transcript, of which 94 percent of remarks were positive and constructive.
2023_023_portrait_of_a_graduate_data_gat.page:
Purpose
The exercise was launched because outside experts such as Tony Wagner emphasize seeking input from the stakeholders most influenced by district policy, because the strategic plan refresh surfaced a call for stronger student voice, and because the Board had asked for a clearer measure of success from a student perspective. The stated goal was to identify what traits should be visible in students if the District is delivering on its promise of a world class education.

Sample

| Group | Method | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Parents | 3-question open-ended survey | 308 completed surveys; 60+ pages of transcripts; 24,000+ words; 94% positive and constructive remarks |
| Principals | 45-minute discussion | All-principals K-12 meeting |
| Students | 30-minute discussions | 4 high schools, 3 middle schools, 4 elementary, 1 preschool; 16 total classrooms; 320+ students |

Core Question Progression
Participants were asked what the best of what the District is doing to date is; what the most critical hard and soft skills are that should be fostered before students leave; and what the secret sauce is that should mark a Troy graduate as an adult.

Findings
Students, parents and principals showed an almost perfect overlap in stated priorities, and those priorities aligned tightly with the District Strategic Plan. The presentation frames the net conclusion as either District strategy matching parent and student ideals, effective communication of the Pillars to key stakeholders, or both. A Leonard second grader supplied the framing quote: a portrait is two things, a picture of you and the best parts of you.

Twelve Traits of a TSD Graduate
Visionary; Connected; Kind, compassionate, and inclusive; Joyous about discovery; Eager for challenge; Tenacious; Intellectual crackerjack; Adaptable; Self-starter; Good team player; Organized; Confident communicator. Each trait carries a definition plus supporting observations. Recurring student themes include a felt disconnect between classroom content and future degree programs or careers, the primacy of teacher relationships, a preference for project-based exploration over what high schoolers described as informational cramming, and the value of trial-and-error work. Students at the two larger high schools felt caring teachers were more the exception than the rule, while students at TCCHS and IAE identified adult engagement and emotional investment as a primary reason for their success. Parent themes include interpersonal connection, grit, source discernment, intellectual flexibility, organization and time management, and communication across changing media.

Mapping and Takeaways
The twelve traits were mapped to the strategic plan areas of EC to Career, Equity and Well-Being, Deep Learning, and Building Capacity. Six broad takeaways were reported: parents hold clear expectations beyond academic success; students know and appreciate deep learning when they experience it; students recognize the need for broader skill sets; everyone grasps the importance of student-adult connections; the more advanced the grade, the less ideal the educational and skill set delivery; and outstanding adults modeling the strategic ideals exist at every level, making the central challenge expanding those examples until they become the norm.

Next Steps
The Board of Education led the research, analysis and creation of the initial construct. Central Administration is now tasked with integrating the findings into professional development across the organization, which will shift the original structure. The presentation suggests sharing the results in their original form with parents and parent groups, and using the traits as a common Board framework for assessing the impact of new pedagogies and the depth of student work across grade levels and subject areas.
2023_023_portrait_of_a_graduate_data_gat.verbose:
Rationale
The Portrait of a Graduate Data Gathering Summary opens by citing outside experts like Tony Wagner, who continue to emphasize the importance of and value in seeking the input of stakeholders most influenced by district policies and focus, namely students. When feedback was gathered for the strategic plan refresh, the organization said loudly and clearly that stronger student voice was needed as part of building a world class experience for Troy students. The Board had also consistently asked for a clearer measure of success from a student perspective as the central tenets of the strategic plan are executed. The District pursued a Portrait of a Troy Graduate exercise as a way to better identify what student traits should be visible if the District is successfully delivering on its promise of a world class education.

Sample and Method
Parents completed a 3-question open-ended survey: 308 completed surveys, more than 60 pages of transcripts, more than 24,000 words, with 94% positive and constructive remarks. Principals participated in a 45-minute discussion at an all-principals K-12 meeting. Students took part in 30-minute discussions across 4 high schools, 3 middle schools, 4 elementary schools and 1 preschool, comprising 16 total classrooms and more than 320 students. The core question progression asked what the best of what the District is doing to date is; what the most critical hard and soft skills are that should be fostered and developed in students before they leave; and, as an adult, what the secret sauce is that should mark a Troy graduate.

Consensus
The presentation reports a near perfect consensus among students, parents and principals, describing an almost perfect overlap in stated priorities that were in tight alignment with the District Strategic Plan. The stated net conclusion is that either District strategy is in line with parent and student ideals, the District has effectively communicated the value of the Pillars to key stakeholder groups, or both. Framing the concept, Karl asked how a portrait differs from a regular picture of someone, and a Leonard second grader answered that a portrait is two things, a picture of you and the best parts of you.

The Twelve Traits
Visionary: can confidently connect formal education and student experiences to the real world and to immediate and long-term futures. Highlight educational experiences almost always made strong connections between subject material and reality, and students described aha moments when those connections were made. Students, particularly high schoolers, often described a disconnect between classroom work and how learning applies to a specific degree program or career, and complained that career planning was disconnected from academics.
Connected: a person who has built meaningful relationships with peers and adults and understands the deep value in those connections. In a world recently marked by isolation and a generation trapped in social media, parents were emphatic about a school experience that builds strong interpersonal relationships for social and emotional stability as well as career advancement. Students at all grade levels also spoke about feeling connected to peers and teachers. High schoolers held teacher relationships up as one of the most important elements of academic and social success, tied to whether they were confident their teachers cared about them as people. In the two larger high schools, students felt caring teachers were more the exception than the rule, while at TCCHS and IAE students identified adult engagement, including emotional investment, as a primary reason for their success.
Kind, compassionate, and inclusive: intrinsically treats others with kindness, respect and fairness. These themes were prominent in parent responses, which tied them to interpersonal skills and broader productive citizenship. Asked what a satisfied employer might see in someone that would suggest a Troy origin, students said they want to be recognized as people who care about and take care of those around them. Both groups stressed recognizing and valuing differences in an increasingly multicultural world.
Joyous about discovery: an enthusiastic lifelong learner, curious about the world and eager to explore new topics and ventures, often just for fun. Parents want children who continue to grow intellectually because they value learning for its own sake. Students did not name this as a desired future differentiator but demonstrated joy, curiosity and excitement about past opportunities to explore on their own terms, experiment and learn by trial and error. The summary paraphrases a common student sentiment: graduates should want to learn something because it fascinates them, not because it is going to be on the test.
Eager for challenge: excited to tackle any challenge and unafraid of Big Hairy Audacious Goals. The trait describes someone bold and confident whom people ask to lead a difficult situation. For parents this linked tightly to tenacity and grit; for students it was more about who they want to be and how they want to be viewed. Ambitious student projects outside core academics, such as Charity Week, are highly valued because they let students tackle a BHAG and see results greater than they thought themselves capable of, breeding confidence for future ones.
Tenacious: marked by grit, a determination to work through challenges and persevere to resolution, and adept in situations requiring productive struggle. Parents worry about educational environments or teaching styles that spoon feed information or provide easy assistance. For students at every grade level tenacity is highly valued, and one of the most commonly desired employer-identified traits was confidence that a Troy graduate given a task will figure out how to make it happen and will not stop pressing until the goal is reached.
Intellectual crackerjack: proficient at drawing meaningful conclusions and developing implications from informational sources, data, research and people, an adept synthesizer of input. One parent described wanting their child to have the intellectual skills to understand reality, while most described recognizing the validity of information sources, drawing conclusions from trustworthy pieces, and adjusting them as new valid information appears. Rather than learning about things, these parents want students taught how to explore, discern and develop their own informed perspectives. Students describe wanting to be seen as smart because they know how to gather good data and figure things out, one reason large, in-depth, longer-deadline projects were a perennial favorite way of learning.
Adaptable: possesses the flexibility to incorporate new information and the willingness to pivot when necessary or beneficial. Many parents railed against intellectual rigidity. Students did not name this as a desired trait but repeatedly held up assignments requiring trial and error or a pivot as situations where their learning went into hyperdrive, saying the process of figuring it out and adjusting from initial errors shifted learning from short-term cramming to long-term, deeper understanding.
Self-starter: confident and willing to tackle deep, complex projects with little assistance. Parents framed this as the ability to take on individual projects and manage them effectively. Students value collaborative work but also want regular opportunities to execute multi-week, multi-layered projects on their own, both for higher education and work and for the control over what they research or create. High schoolers in particular described most current classwork as informational cramming aimed at retention testing rather than applied mastery, and turned repeatedly to project-based exploration as their preferred approach.
Good team player: can lead or contribute as a group member with ease, understanding interpersonal dynamics, allocation of responsibilities, intellectual humility when others have higher expertise, and how to move a group forward productively and positively. Parents and students at all grade levels recognized the need to master group work. All stakeholder groups noted the binary temptation to see a student as either driving a group project or leeching off it, and observed that meaningful contribution means continuous curiosity so that students who did not start as the expert can become one. Students consistently asked for a mix of team and individual work.
Organized: possesses top-notch organization, time management and project management skills. Parents begged the District for help in this area to emphasize how important the skill is. Students were less likely to list it as a desired trait, though some at every level wanted to hone organizational skills before graduating, and noted that complex, longer-term projects require mapping out the entire process and completing steps in a timely manner.
Confident communicator: able to easily convey ideas, information and their own perspective through one-on-one conversation, writing and a variety of interactive media. Described as universally valued, with both parents and students wanting communications practice incorporated across every aspect of a student's academic career, and parents attentive to the constantly changing and fractured communications landscape.

Mapping to the Strategic Plan
The twelve traits were mapped against the strategic plan areas listed as EC to Career, Equity and Well-Being, Deep Learning, and Building Capacity.

Six Broad Takeaways
Parents have clear, powerful expectations of the District that go well beyond academic success. Students know and appreciate deep learning when they experience it. Students recognize the need to develop broader skill sets for later success. Everyone grasps the extreme importance of strong connections between students and District adults. Currently, the more advanced the grade, the less ideal the educational and skill set delivery. At every grade level there are outstanding adults modeling the strategic ideals, making the biggest challenge expanding those examples until they become the norm.

So Now What
As requested, the Board of Education was given the opportunity to lead the research, analysis and creation of the initial Portrait of a Graduate construct. Central Administration is now tasked with integrating the findings into professional development across the organization in a way staff can digest and that becomes part of the life blood of the District, so the original structure will shift. The presentation notes possible value in sharing the results in their original form with parents and parent groups so they understand the broader educational and personal goals for all students, and suggests the Board could use the traits as a common framework for assessing the impact of new pedagogies and the depth of student work across grade levels and subject areas.

2023_024_m071823bdmtg.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education meeting held July 18, 2023 at the Administration Building, 4400 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 9:30 a.m. and adjourned at 9:58 a.m. The Board adopted a seven-item consent agenda and approved five personnel resolutions, including two-year probationary administrative contracts for Larson Middle School Principal Brian Zawislak and Communications Director Kendra Montante, contract extensions through June 30, 2025 for building administrators and the three assistant superintendents, and an extension of the Superintendent's contract running July 1, 2023 through June 30, 2028. Every recorded vote was 6 yes, 0 no, with Mrs. Alic absent.
2023_024_m071823bdmtg.page:
Attendance
The meeting was held at the Troy School District Administration Building, 4400 Livernois. President Schmidt called it to order at 9:30 a.m. Present with Mr. Schmidt were Board members Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart and Wilson; Mrs. Alic was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Fulcher, Keyser and West; and approximately 4 other members of the audience.
